title: How Long Should Christians Date Before Marriage? The Question That Could Save You Years of Heartbreak
paragraphs: How Long Should Christians Date Before Marriage? The Question That Could Save You Years of Heartbreak

The Bible never gives Christians a mandatory dating timeline—but it gives us something far more demanding: a way to discern whether the person holding your hand is actually prepared to walk with you toward Christ for the rest of your life.
Maybe you came here hoping for a number.
Six months.
One year.
Two years.
Maybe you secretly want permission to marry the person you love.
Or maybe something inside you has been uneasy for months, and you are hoping Scripture will finally say what your heart has been afraid to admit.
So here is the first truth we need to establish before emotions take over:
The Bible does not tell Christians, “Date for exactly this many months before marriage.”

There is no biblical command saying twelve months is holy and six months is reckless. There is no verse establishing an eighteen-month courtship requirement. Modern dating as we practice it did not exist in precisely the same social form in the biblical world.
So anyone claiming that God has commanded every Christian couple to date for a specific number of months is going beyond what Scripture actually says.
But that does not mean Scripture leaves us directionless.
In fact, the Bible asks questions far more serious than, “How long have you been together?”
It asks:
Who are you becoming together?
That question changes everything.
Because you can date someone for three years and still refuse to see what is directly in front of you.

And you can spend less time with another person yet approach marriage with extraordinary seriousness, mature Christian counsel, transparent conversations, observable character, sexual integrity, financial honesty, theological agreement, and genuine submission to Christ.
Time matters.
But time alone proves almost nothing.
A calendar cannot repent.
A calendar cannot tell the truth.
A calendar cannot demonstrate self-control.
A calendar cannot reveal whether someone loves Jesus when nobody is watching.
A calendar cannot guarantee covenant faithfulness.
You are not ultimately trying to discover whether you can survive twelve months of dating.

You are discerning whether the two of you should enter a covenant intended to survive sickness, disappointment, financial pressure, temptation, aging, conflict, grief, unanswered prayers, changing bodies, sleepless nights, parenting pressures, failures, victories, and all the ordinary Tuesdays nobody photographs.
That is why Christian dating cannot merely be secular dating with Bible verses attached.
The destination changes the journey.

Marriage, biblically understood, is not simply the moment two people decide that their chemistry is strong enough to justify permanence. Jesus points back to creation when speaking about marriage: “the two shall become one flesh” (Matthew 19:5), and then declares, “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Matthew 19:6).
That is covenant language.
Weighty language.
Forever-shaped language.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely:
How long should we date?
The deeper question becomes:
Have we dated long enough, wisely enough, honestly enough, and purely enough to discern whether entering that covenant would honor Jesus Christ?
Paul gives us one of the clearest boundaries when discussing remarriage in 1 Corinthians 7:39. He says a believer is free to marry whom she wishes, but adds the decisive qualification:
“only in the Lord.”
The Greek phrase is beautifully concise:
μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ — monon en kyriō
Literally, “only in the Lord.”
Those few words destroy one of the most dangerous fantasies in Christian dating:
Maybe I can change them after we get married.
Maybe they will eventually become serious about Jesus.
Maybe after the wedding they will start praying.
Maybe after children arrive they will suddenly want church.
Maybe eventually they will stop mocking my convictions.
Maybe someday they will surrender to Christ.
Maybe.
Maybe.
Maybe.
But marriage is far too sacred to build on a hypothetical conversion.
You are not the Holy Spirit.
And dating someone should never become a missionary strategy disguised as romance.

Paul elsewhere warns believers not to become “unequally yoked” with unbelievers (2 Corinthians 6:14). In its immediate context, that passage addresses compromising partnership between believers and unbelief rather than serving merely as a standalone dating rule. Yet its underlying concern about binding spiritual partnership fits naturally alongside Paul's explicit instruction that marriage be “only in the Lord.” Scripture does not envision Christian marriage as one person pursuing Christ while the other remains spiritually opposed to Him.
And this is where someone reading this may already feel uncomfortable.
Because the person you love may be kind.
Funny.
Attractive.
Generous.
Successful.
They may respect your Christianity.
They may even attend church with you occasionally.
But the question is not merely whether they respect your faith.
Do they belong to Christ?
There is an enormous difference between someone who tolerates Jesus because they love you and someone who loves you because they first belong to Jesus.
Do not confuse proximity to Christianity with surrender to Christ.
Someone can know worship songs without worshiping.
Someone can attend church without being converted.
Someone can post Bible verses while living in deliberate rebellion against God.
Someone can say, “I believe in God,” while Jesus remains functionally irrelevant to every major decision they make.
Christian marriage needs something deeper than religious compatibility.
It needs two sinners who understand that neither one is the Savior.
That matters because eventually the butterflies become quieter.
Eventually you see each other tired.
Eventually someone gets sick.
Eventually money becomes stressful.
Eventually one person says something cruel.
Eventually disappointment enters the room.
Eventually sexual attraction fluctuates.
Eventually you discover habits that dating allowed each other to hide.
Eventually marriage reveals that you did not marry an ideal.
You married a sinner.
And so did they.
Then the question becomes:
Where do two sinners go when they hurt each other?
If both belong to Jesus, they have somewhere to go.
To the cross.
Not merely to communication techniques.
Not merely to compatibility tests.
Not merely to romantic memories.
To Christ.
The Christian marriage is not sustained because two flawless people finally found each other.
It is sustained by two imperfect people continually being brought under the lordship, forgiveness, correction, grace, and transforming power of Jesus Christ.
This is why one of the most important things dating should reveal is not whether someone ever fails.
They will.
So will you.
Dating should reveal what they do when their failure is exposed.
Watch carefully.
When they hurt you, do they repent—or manipulate?
When corrected, do they become humble—or defensive?
When they sin, do they confess—or hide?
When confronted, do they take responsibility—or somehow make everything your fault?
When angry, do they remain self-controlled—or become frightening?
When nobody applauds them, do they still serve?
When temptation appears, what happens to their convictions?
When you establish physical boundaries, do they protect those boundaries with you—or continually negotiate them downward?
That last question deserves more attention than many Christian couples want to give it.
Because sometimes what Christians call “chemistry” is actually temptation being repeatedly fed.
Scripture does not treat sexual holiness casually.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is πορνεία — porneia, a broad New Testament term for sexually immoral behavior.
Notice the startling clarity.
People often pray:
“God, show me Your will for this relationship.”
And Scripture answers at least part of that prayer before you ever receive a mysterious sign:
God's will is your sanctification.
So if your relationship consistently pulls both of you toward sexual compromise, secrecy, rationalization, and disobedience, you should not merely ask whether you love each other.
Ask whether the relationship is helping either of you love Christ more faithfully.
And hear this carefully, especially if shame is already rising inside you:
Sexual failure does not place you beyond the reach of Jesus.
Maybe you already crossed boundaries.
Maybe you slept together.
Maybe you have been living together.
Maybe there are messages you would panic if your pastor saw.
Maybe you knew exactly where the boundary was and walked across it anyway.
The Gospel is not the announcement that clean people can approach Jesus.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be washed.
Paul wrote to people whose pasts included serious sexual sin and then said something breathtaking:
“And such were some of you. But you were washed…” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Were.
That word carries hope.
Your sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have to write the ending.
Repentance is not pretending the sin never happened. Repentance turns toward God because Christ has made forgiveness possible through His death and resurrection.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not cheap grace that says sin does not matter.
Costly grace that says sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so astonishing that repentant sinners can come home.
So should Christians date three months?
Six months?
A year?
Two years?
Here is the answer many people will find frustrating because it refuses to manufacture a command God never gave:
There is no universally biblical minimum dating period.
But wisdom normally refuses both reckless haste and endless ambiguity.
A couple considering marriage needs enough time and real-life exposure for character to become observable rather than merely advertised.
Dating is partly the season when promises get tested against patterns.
Everybody can perform for a little while.
Eventually patterns speak.
You need to see more than someone's romantic side.
See how they treat their parents.
See how they treat waiters.
See how they treat people who cannot advance their career.
See what happens when plans collapse.
See how they handle money.
See whether they keep commitments.
See how they speak about former partners.
See whether they can apologize without adding, “but you…”
See whether they forgive.
See whether they serve.
See whether they work.
See whether they tell the truth when lying would be easier.
See what happens when you disagree.
See whether their Christianity exists outside Sunday morning.
And let them see the real you too.
Because discernment cannot happen when both people are dating fictional versions of each other.
You are not trying to “win” marriage.
You are trying to discern it.
That means important conversations should happen before vows make their consequences permanent.
Talk about children.
Talk about whether you want them and how you understand parenting.
Talk about money.
Not theoretically.
Debt.
Income.
Spending.
Giving.
Saving.
Financial obligations.
Talk about church.
Talk about doctrine.
Talk about prayer.
Talk about sex and expectations without using the conversation as an excuse to arouse each other.
Talk about pornography and sexual history with appropriate honesty and grace.
Talk about family expectations.
Talk about careers.
Talk about where you might live.
Talk about conflict.
Talk about emotional wounds.
Talk about expectations surrounding household responsibilities.
Talk about ministry.
Talk about what submission to Christ actually looks like when the two of you want different things.
And bring mature believers into the process.
One of the great dangers of romantic love is that two people can create an emotional universe in which they continually confirm each other's preferred interpretation of reality.
“We prayed about it.”
Good.
But prayer should never become spiritual language for refusing counsel.
Proverbs repeatedly commends wise counsel. Mature Christians who know you well may notice what infatuation makes difficult to see.
Your pastor does not need to choose your spouse.
Your parents do not automatically possess infallible judgment.
Your friends should not control your future.
But if every mature, godly person who knows both of you is expressing the same serious concern, humility should at least make you listen.
Sometimes love needs witnesses.
Sometimes what you call persecution is actually protection.
And sometimes people around you are wrong.
Which is why everything ultimately returns to Scripture, prayer, character, wisdom, and Christ.
There is another side to this conversation, though.
Some Christians are not rushing marriage.
They are endlessly postponing it.
Years pass.
“We're still discerning.”
But nothing changes.
They function emotionally like spouses.
Sometimes sexually like spouses.
They expect exclusivity like spouses.
They consume enormous portions of each other's lives like spouses.
Yet one person continually refuses covenant.
There can be legitimate reasons to wait: age, maturity, education, finances, family circumstances, unresolved issues, safety concerns, or the need for serious spiritual growth.
But indefinite dating should not automatically be praised as wisdom.
Sometimes endless dating is simply fear wearing the clothes of discernment.

If you have had sufficient time to know one another, both belong to Christ, mature believers affirm the relationship, serious incompatibilities have been addressed, you share a biblical understanding of marriage, there are no unresolved red flags requiring attention, and both genuinely desire covenant marriage…
Eventually discernment requires a decision.
Marriage is not a reward for finally eliminating every possible risk.
You cannot.
There is no dating period long enough to guarantee you will never experience pain.
There is no premarital questionnaire capable of predicting every future version of yourselves.
There is no compatibility score high enough to remove the need for grace.
At some point Christian marriage still requires faith.
Not blind faith in another human being.
Faith in God while making a wise, sober covenant with another imperfect believer.
And perhaps the person who most needs this article is not asking, “How long should Christians date?”
Maybe your real question is:
“How much longer should I ignore what God has already shown me?”
You keep extending the relationship because ending it feels unbearable.
You have invested years.
Your families know each other.
Your photos are everywhere.
Everyone expects the wedding.
You remember how beautiful the beginning was.
And you keep hoping the person from the beginning will come back.
But now there is manipulation.
Repeated betrayal.
Controlling behavior.
Spiritual contempt.
Persistent dishonesty.
Sexual pressure.
Cruelty.
Threats.
Or a pattern that makes you afraid.
Please understand this: marriage does not magically sanctify dangerous patterns.
A wedding ring is not a treatment for abuse.
Do not marry someone because you are afraid nobody else will ever choose you.
Do not marry someone because you are terrified of starting over.
Do not marry someone because you have already had sex and now believe marriage is the only way God can redeem what happened.
You do not purchase forgiveness by marrying the person you sinned with.
Christ purchased forgiveness with His blood.
Repent.
Receive grace.
Then make the next decision in wisdom.
Maybe that means rebuilding the relationship differently.
Maybe that means counseling and accountability.
Maybe that means slowing down.
Maybe that means ending it.
But do not let yesterday's sin become tomorrow's prison.
And please remember something else the church sometimes communicates badly:
Singleness is not God's waiting room.
Marriage is good.
But marriage is not salvation.
A spouse cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
Paul himself speaks with remarkable dignity about singleness in 1 Corinthians 7. Jesus Christ lived the perfectly fulfilled human life without marrying.
So your value is not measured by whether somebody proposes.
You do not become complete when another human chooses you.
If you are in Christ, your deepest identity has already been spoken over you by Someone infinitely greater.
You belong to Jesus.
That means you can afford to walk away from relationships that require you to betray Him in order to keep them.
Read that again.
You can afford to lose someone you wanted rather than lose yourself trying to make an idol stay.
Maybe that is the sentence you came here for.
Because some relationships become idols so gradually that we do not notice the altar being built.
First you compromise a boundary.
Then another.
Then you stop telling Christian friends what is really happening.
Then prayer becomes uncomfortable.
Then Scripture feels accusatory.
Then you avoid people who challenge the relationship.
Then eventually you are no longer asking:
“Lord, is this relationship pleasing to You?”
You are asking:
“Lord, please approve what I have already decided.”
That is not discernment.
That is negotiation.
Jesus deserves more than veto power over your worst decisions.
He is Lord.
κύριος — kyrios.
Lord.
Master.
The One with rightful authority.
And that brings us back to Paul's deceptively simple phrase:
μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ — monon en kyriō — “only in the Lord.”
Your dating life belongs there too.
In the Lord.
Your attraction.
In the Lord.
Your sexuality.
In the Lord.
Your loneliness.
In the Lord.
Your wedding dreams.
In the Lord.
Your heartbreak.
In the Lord.
Your future.
In the Lord.
Everything.
Because Christianity is not about squeezing Jesus into the relationship you have chosen.
It is about laying the relationship before the Jesus who chose you.
So how long should Christians date before marriage?

Long enough to discern character beyond chemistry. Long enough to have the conversations infatuation wants to postpone. Long enough for trusted believers to observe the relationship. Long enough to identify serious patterns rather than isolated performances. Long enough to know that you share genuine faith in Christ and a biblical understanding of covenant. Long enough to pursue marriage soberly rather than impulsively—but not so indefinitely that “discernment” becomes an excuse for enjoying marital-level attachment while perpetually refusing covenant.
That may be months for some couples and considerably longer for others.
Scripture gives no stopwatch.
It gives something better.
Wisdom.
Holiness.
Community.
Truth.
Covenant.
And Christ.
And maybe right now you realize you have been measuring your relationship by the wrong question.
Not:
“How long have we dated?”
But:
“Is this relationship teaching us to love Jesus more—or teaching us how much compromise we can survive?”
Be honest.
If that exposed something you have been hiding, don't perform spirituality here.
Your testimony may become another person's warning, courage, or hope.

Because after all the questions about timing, compatibility, attraction, engagement rings, wedding dates, and happily-ever-after dreams, one question will remain when everything temporary has fallen away:
Did this love help you follow Jesus—or did you keep asking Jesus to follow your love?
